scope: Manual comparison of fourteen remaining deconvolution interfaces, including exact Fourier signs, strict-versus-nonstrict packing, observation-law sieve conditions and the distinction between a signed raw estimator and its probability-valued approximation.

rows.query: Inspect InformationTheory/KullbackLeibler/Basic klDiv and its absolute-continuity, log-likelihood integrability and mass-correction branches; compare the two separate source neighborhood inequalities
rows.result: For probability measures with the proper absolute continuity and integrability, klDiv has the source's ordered log-likelihood expectation; the additional raw second log-ratio moment is not part of that divergence definition.
rows.gap: Identify the density log-ratio with the ordered library likelihood ratio and construct the neighborhood imposing both KL and raw second-moment bounds.

comparisons.D10: The order is P then Q and the integrand is log(f_P/f_Q) under P, not the reverse divergence. For probabilities the library's mass correction cancels, but absolute continuity and integrability must be verified to use the finite branch. Require KL<=epsilon^2 and separately integral (log(f_P/f_Q))^2 dP<=epsilon^2 for epsilon>0, with Q in the source's absolutely continuous probability class. The second expression is the raw second moment, not the centered log-ratio variance. A zero density denominator or a nonintegrable real log must not be interpreted through a totalized zero integral; no Hellinger condition is substituted.

rows.query: Search Topology for packing numbers; inspect Metric.packingNumber, its extended-cardinality supremum and Metric.IsSeparated's defining strict extended-distance inequality
rows.result: The library supplies an extended packing cardinality for strictly greater-than-radius separated sets, whereas the source permits equality at epsilon; this is a related packing interface with a material boundary difference.
rows.gap: Define or relate the source's nonstrict epsilon-separated packing number and instantiate the chosen Hellinger or L1 metric without losing boundary cases.

comparisons.D27: For epsilon>0 the source counts a subset of B with pairwise distance at least epsilon. Metric.packingNumber at the same radius requires distance strictly greater than epsilon and can differ even on a finite set with two points exactly epsilon apart. It returns an extended natural supremum, not a selected maximal finite set; finiteness and attainment need their own conditions when interpreting a finite entropy. The metric argument d can be Hellinger or L1 and is distinct from ambient dimension d. The source's Hellinger convention has no extra 1/sqrt(2) factor, so metric scaling also must be preserved.

rows.query: Inspect klDiv, Metric.packingNumber with its strict-separation caveat, Tendsto and real exp/log; compare every rate, sieve, entropy and prior-mass clause of (4.1)
rows.result: The KL, packing and convergence ingredients are available but do not package the deconvolution sieve or prior-mass hypotheses; the packing boundary difference must be resolved before transporting an entropy bound.
rows.gap: Assemble the observation-law moment sieve and all three entropy/prior-mass inequalities with the exact rate sequence and induced prior interpretation.

comparisons.D11: Require epsilon-tilde_n>=sqrt(log n/n) and epsilon-tilde_n tending to zero, positive c_1,...,c_4,K-prime and P_n contained in the signal laws whose induced observation law mu_Y has M_{4+delta}<=K-prime epsilon-tilde_n^(-2). The entropy is log D(epsilon-tilde_n,F(P_n),d)<=c_1 n epsilon-tilde_n^2 using the source's nonstrict packing and density identification. The outside prior mass bound is c_3 exp(-(c_2+4)n epsilon-tilde_n^2), while KL small-ball mass is at least c_4 exp(-c_2 n epsilon-tilde_n^2) around P_0Y, including the raw second log moment. The prior is specified on signal/mixing parameters, so the observation-law event uses its induced law. These are hypotheses of Theorem 4.1 and conclusions asserted by Theorems 4.2/4.4, not automatically inherited hypotheses in every later reference.

rows.query: Inspect Measure/CharacteristicFunction/Basic charFun's positive imaginary exponent and Analysis/Calculus/IteratedDeriv/Defs iteratedDeriv with a real scalar domain and complex codomain
rows.result: The characteristic function matches the source Fourier convention for an error probability density, and iteratedDeriv represents the integer derivatives of its reciprocal; nonvanishing and differentiability remain required hypotheses.
rows.gap: Identify the error density transform with its characteristic function and justify the real-variable iterated derivatives of the nonvanishing complex reciprocal.

comparisons.D29: For every real t, nonzero abs f-hat_epsilon(t) permits r_epsilon(t)=1/f-hat_epsilon(t). Treat r as a function from R to C and use iteratedDeriv with scalar field R; no holomorphic extension in t is assumed. At order zero the operation gives r itself. An l-times differentiable transform with no zeros provides the route to differentiability of the reciprocal, which needs proof rather than relying on a derivative's totalized fallback. The transform uses the positive imaginary exponent without a 2pi factor, and the source's inverse convention is handled separately.

rows.query: Inspect Analysis/Convolution function convolution, Probability/CDF cdf and the integral definitions against the rescaled scalar kernel and projected product-kernel bias
rows.result: Ordinary function convolution and the signal probability CDF have matching ingredients; the potentially signed product-kernel projection is not a probability pushforward and needs its own construction.
rows.gap: Construct the rescaled and projected possibly signed kernels and define the CDF-minus-convolution bias with the source's signal projection convention.

comparisons.D7: For h>0 use K_h(x)=h^(-1)K(x/h) and b_F(h)=F-F*K_h, retaining that sign. The multidimensional kernel is the product over coordinate kernels, with rescaling in each coordinate, and its projection along a Euclidean unit v is convolved with the one-dimensional CDF of the projected signal law. Library convolution has integrand f(t)g(x-t); use scalar multiplication and real volume, supplying convolution integrability or a justified commutation to the chosen bias expression. K and its projection can be signed, so ordinary probability Measure.map/cdf cannot stand in for their signed-density construction. Condition (a) is a separate theorem-branch requirement, not built into the supplied-kernel definition.

rows.query: Search Analysis for fractional derivatives and Sobolev interfaces; inspect charFun, explicit-character fourierIntegral, Integrable and eLpNorm against the direction-uniform weighted Fourier and fractional-derivative L1 conditions
rows.result: Fourier integration and L1 finiteness can represent the two source bounds; the inspected Sobolev/Bessel framework is not an exact API for this direction-uniform one-sided complex multiplier construction.
rows.gap: Construct each projected fractional derivative with an explicit complex-power branch and prove both L1 bounds uniformly over Euclidean unit directions.

comparisons.D5: The mixing law is absolutely continuous with finite first moment and has alpha>0 such that max_v integral |t|^alpha |mu-hat_0X(t v)| dt and max_v norm_1(D^alpha f_0X,v) are finite. Retain the same unit direction throughout each expression and require uniform finite bounds, not merely a finite value for each direction. The fractional derivative is the inverse Fourier transform of (-i t)^alpha mu-hat_0X(t v) with the source's positive-forward/negative-inverse signs; a complex fractional-power branch is not specified in the main text and must not be silently chosen. L1 fractional regularity is not replaced by L2 Sobolev membership. These assumptions occur only in the additional-regularity branches, and finite sup bounds alone do not prove attainment of the displayed maxima.

rows.query: Inspect Integrable, Real.rpow, Real.exp and the constant-coefficient HolderOnWith definition; compare the source's point-dependent L0 envelope and weighted envelope-ratio integral
rows.result: The integrability and weighted real-power expressions are available; a standard HolderOnWith constant does not match the point-dependent envelope, and the ratio at density zeros is unresolved by the source.
rows.gap: Define the global envelope increment condition and exponential ratio moment with the precise alpha-dependent integer and exponent constraints and an explicit interpretation at density zeros.

comparisons.D20: For the supplied alpha>0 choose 0<upsilon<=1, an L1 function L0, the smallest integer m>=max(2,(alpha+2)/2), and R>=2m/upsilon. The bound is |f_0X(x+zeta)-f_0X(x)|<=L0(x)|zeta|^upsilon for every real x,zeta, with no global constant replacing L0(x). Also require finiteness of integral exp(|x|/2) f_0X(x)(L0(x)/f_0X(x))^R dx. At f_0X(x)=0 the displayed ratio has no stated convention; using real division's zero fallback would impose an interpretation absent from the source. The norm-like name of a Holder condition does not remove either the integrable envelope or the exponential weight.

rows.query: Inspect Integrable, MemLp, explicit-character fourierIntegral and Function.support; compare the source's even kernel, Fourier support and plateau conditions
rows.result: L1/L2 membership and Fourier support are representable with checked declarations; no verified ready-made kernel satisfying this complete source-normalized condition was identified.
rows.gap: Assemble the symmetric kernel's integrability, first absolute weighted moment and exact Fourier support-and-plateau conditions using the source normalization.

comparisons.D6: Require K in L1 and L2 under real Lebesgue measure and x times K(x) in L1, hence an integrable absolute first weighted kernel. K is symmetric as an even scalar function. Its positive-exponent Fourier transform vanishes outside [-2,2] and equals one throughout [-1,1], including the stated closed boundaries. Nonzero support containment can represent the Fourier support restriction, with continuity justifying equivalent closed-support wording where needed. The source does not require K>=0, and this condition belongs to the additional-regularity branch under Assumption 3.2 rather than every use of a bias kernel.

rows.query: Inspect charFun, iteratedDeriv, Integrable and IsBigOWith including its filter argument; compare the reciprocal derivative growth orders zero and one in (3.2)
rows.result: The transform, derivative and all-input growth predicates have checked representations; they do not supply a nonvanishing ordinary-smooth error model or establish its reciprocal derivative bounds.
rows.gap: Define the absolutely continuous finite-first-moment error class and prove nonvanishing plus global reciprocal derivative growth with the correct order-dependent exponents.

comparisons.D4: The scalar error law is absolutely continuous and has finite first moment, its transform has no zeros on R, and for l=0,1 the complex modulus of r_epsilon^(l)(t) is bounded by a constant times (1+|t|)^(beta-l) for every t, for some beta>0. IsBigOWith on the principal filter of the whole real domain can encode that global inequality; atTop alone would drop negative and bounded t. Real-variable iterated derivatives must exist. This is a bound on the reciprocal transform through order one, not Theorem 5.1's separate decay assumptions on derivatives of the transform itself through order two.

rows.query: Inspect explicit-character Fourier integration and integrability, and compare the Bessel Sobolev definition with the source's two exponential tilts and homogeneous Fourier weight
rows.result: The two tilted Fourier integrals and their weighted squared magnitudes are expressible; standard unweighted Sobolev membership does not include the source's pair of exponential tilts or its exact homogeneous weight.
rows.gap: Construct both exponentially tilted density transforms and establish their homogeneous alpha-weighted Fourier square integrability under the source convention.

comparisons.D19: For the same alpha>0 impose the weighted integral for both b=-1/2 and b=+1/2. The Fourier transform is applied to x↦exp(b x) f_0X(x), then |t|^(2alpha) multiplies its squared complex modulus before integration. This is not the Fourier transform of f shifted along the real axis, the unweighted Sobolev ball, or direction-projected L1 regularity. The existence and intended meaning of the tilted transforms and finite integrals need appropriate integrability, not totalized integral zeros. No 1+t^2 weight or absent sign of b is substituted.

rows.query: Inspect Analysis/Distribution/Sobolev MemSobolev and its Bessel multiplier, explicit-character fourierIntegral and Integrable; compare the coordinate-sum anisotropic source bound
rows.result: The library has Bessel-potential Sobolev membership, but the source specifies an anisotropic Fourier norm ball with a coordinate-sum weight and exact radius, requiring separate norm and normalization comparisons.
rows.gap: Define the source's anisotropic weighted Fourier ball and prove any relation to library Sobolev membership without changing its weight, radius or added probability-moment intersection.

comparisons.D21: Start with integrable real functions on R^d and require sum_{j=1}^d integral |f-hat(t)|^2(1+t_j^2)^alpha_j dt<=L^2. The coordinate weights are summed, not multiplied, and setting all alpha_j=alpha retains that sum rather than automatically replacing it by (1+norm t squared)^alpha. MemSobolev uses a tempered-distribution Bessel potential and only a membership predicate; Fourier sign/2pi conventions and norm equivalence constants must be tracked before asserting an exact ball match. Theorem 5.1 separately intersects this class with a bounded-first-moment probability class. The printed simultaneous H_d notation in the isotropic sentence does not supply a new Holder-ball definition.

rows.query: Inspect Fourier integration, iteratedDeriv, IsBigO and exp/sqrt against the source's partial cutoff specification and rapid derivative decay; retain its unresolved external construction
rows.result: The Fourier bound, all-order derivatives and two-sided rapid-decay predicates can be stated, but the source's cited cutoff construction and transition values are not supplied by these declarations.
rows.gap: Specify a cutoff satisfying the exact stated plateau, support and Fourier derivative bounds, retaining the external construction and transition interval as unresolved source data.

comparisons.D22: Tau maps R to [0,1], equals one for |u|<1 and zero for |u|>17/15; no unique values on the transition or a new boundary convention are invented. Its transform obeys |tau-hat(x)|<=(16^2/15) exp(-sqrt(|x|/15)), with the divisor inside the square root. Every integer derivative order i exists and has O(|x|^(-nu)) decay for each nu>0 as |x| becomes large, requiring a two-sided large-absolute-value filter rather than only positive infinity. K is this transform in the estimator. The cited external theorem is not imported, and a generic smooth cutoff is not assumed to achieve these particular constants and bounds.

rows.query: Inspect explicit-character fourierIntegral, charFun, dirac empirical measures and Bochner integral; compare the complete inverse deconvolution integral and bandwidth
rows.result: The empirical characteristic function and explicitly normalized inverse Fourier integral can be constructed; the product kernel, error reciprocal and estimator's integrability and real/signed interpretation require additional work.
rows.gap: Assemble the raw deconvolution estimator with the exact bandwidth, product factors and inverse-transform normalization, without adding positivity or a real-part projection.

comparisons.D23: Use b_n=n^(-1/(2 beta d+1)) and phi_n(t)=n^(-1) sum exp(i t dot Y_j), obtainable from the empirical measure's charFun. Multiply by the product of rescaled-kernel Fourier factors and the coordinatewise product r_epsilon, then integrate exp(-i t dot x) times that product over R^d with factor (2pi)^(-d). The forward convention has no 2pi in its exponent; configure fourierIntegral's character/pairing accordingly rather than accepting default scaling. K is tau-hat from the prior cutoff passage. The displayed integral is retained without inserting a real-part operator, and its nonnegativity is not claimed. In Theorem 5.2 standard Laplace noise gives beta=2 and hence the stated exponent 1/(4d+1), without using the conflicting following extension prose.

rows.query: Inspect eLpNorm at exponent one, Bochner integral and IsBigO; compare the probability-valued approximate minimizer against the raw estimator's signed projected CDF interpretation
rows.result: Projected CDF L1 errors and a deterministic-order slack can be represented, but the checked primitives do not provide a measurable probability-valued near-minimizer of the direction-supremum loss.
rows.gap: Construct the signed raw projected CDFs and a measurable first-moment probability-valued approximate minimizer with one O(n^-1/2) slack valid against every candidate law.

comparisons.D24: For every candidate mu in P_1(R^d), compare the supremum over Euclidean unit v of the L1 difference from the raw projected F to that of the selected probability law, allowing the same O(n^(-1/2)) additive slack independent of the candidate. Define the raw F through its signed density/measure interpretation; it need not be monotone or lie in [0,1], so ProbabilityTheory.cdf of an ordinary positive measure cannot represent it automatically. Finite eLpNorm at one supplies the intended L1 values before real conversion. The selected mu-tilde_1n is a probability measure rather than the possibly signed raw mu-tilde_n; existence, first moments and measurable selection require justification. A generic exact IsMinOn predicate would discard the permitted slack, and the source's O notation is not silently changed to O_P.
